place: Kathmandu — Swayambhunath (Monkey Temple) and Durbar Square
message: Rest day in Kathmandu. Tyler explored Swayambhunath — the Monkey Temple — and Durbar Square this morning, then headed back to the hotel to relax before walking around Thamel in the afternoon. The trek begins tomorrow.

photos.caption: Sunset over Kathmandu from the Monkey Temple hill.
A mother monkey grooming her baby at sunset.
The Swayambhunath stupa, its Buddha eyes watching over the city.
The long staircase climb up to the temple.
A row of prayer wheels at the temple.
A street dog catching a nap on a brick step.

message: Guided tour of Durbar Square with Mr Chet, who taught Tyler about Nepali culture and history — Kathmandu means "wooden city" (many original temples built mainly of wood, some from a single tree) and Nepal means "adopted by guru" — and treated him to a traditional Nepali breakfast for $1. Mr Chet invited him to celebrate the end of Dashain with his family after the trek. A fun, busy start to the day before tomorrow's flight to Lukla.

Tyler in front of the Buddha Tree at Durbar Square.
Black carved wooden windows on a brick temple building.

A temple at Durbar Square covered in pigeons.

The great stupa of Swayambhunath with prayer flags.

message: Day 1 of the trek is underway! Tyler flew into Lukla this morning and trekked on to Monjo, arriving at his lodge this afternoon. The Himalayan adventure has officially begun. Day 1 by the numbers (per his Garmin): 7.82 miles, 2,090 ft of elevation gain, 3 hours 40 minutes — “endless ups and downs, countless donkeys and yaks (and their poop), but also so many beautiful views.”

photos.caption: Snow-capped Himalayan peaks from the plane window.
The Lukla runway at Tenzing-Hillary Airport, mountains all around.
Tyler crossing a suspension bridge on the trail.
Stone lodges along the trail with the mountains behind.
The main dining area at the Monjo lodge.
The dining room stove keeping things cozy.
Lunch at the lodge — dal bhat with all the fixings.
The view from Tyler's room.

message: Day 2 done — Tyler made it to Namche! He trekked up from Monjo, crossing the Dudh Koshi on its long suspension bridges (a little nerve-wracking, especially sharing them with the mule trains) and passing through the Sagarmatha National Park gate along the way. He is settled at the Panorama Lodge overlooking Namche for the next two nights. He met Anna and Frank, an older couple from the Netherlands, and they bonded over Holland — both the Michigan and European kind. Pulse ox was 94% on arrival and he says he feels really strong physically. Day 2 by the numbers (per his Garmin): 3.84 miles, 2,487 ft of elevation gain, 2 hours 12 minutes — a “crazy steep day” with plenty of breaks for water, waiting for the mules (or are they donkeys?) at the suspension bridges, and admiring the views.

photos.caption: The Dudh Koshi river in all its might.
Taboche peak through the valley.
Tyler at a viewpoint with Taboche behind.
One of the long suspension bridges over the Dudh Koshi.
Tyler entering Sagarmatha National Park.

message: Acclimatization day! Tyler was up and hiking at 6am, beating the breakfast crowds to have Hotel Everest View (12,730 ft) nearly to himself. A couple of energy snacks held him over for the climb, with a proper breakfast waiting at the viewpoint — plus coffee at 12,730 ft. Lhotse and Ama Dablam played peek-a-boo through the clouds. The climb up took an hour flat (1.91 miles, 1,339 ft of elevation gain) — “coffee and a view.” The hike back down was “so beautiful,” and spotting some of the BIG ones has him excited for the days ahead.

photos.caption: Lhotse partially hidden behind the clouds.
Ama Dablam peeking through the clouds.
Coffee at 12,730 ft!
The entrance to Hotel Everest View (12,730 ft).

message: Day 4: Namche → Tengboche. The morning started with a breakfast view from the Panorama Lodge — snow-dusted peaks over Namche’s blue rooftops. With Tengboche fully booked, the plan was to push on to Pangboche — but a room opened up in Tengboche after all. Mani stone walls, snowy valleys, and a prayer-flagged chorten marked the trail. Day 4 by the numbers (per his Garmin): 6.47 miles, 2,671 ft of elevation gain, 3 hours 26 minutes moving — “one helluva climb the last couple miles,” with mist and sprinkles, but the rain held off.

photos.caption: The breakfast view from the lodge in Namche.
Tyler by a mani stone wall on the trail.
A snowy valley along the way.
A chorten with prayer flags on the trail.

message: Day 5: Tengboche → Dingboche. Bundled up against the morning cold, Tyler set out around 7 for 6.2 miles of steady uphill — about the same time on trail as previous days. He picked a good lodge here — a bit more expensive, but with an attached bathroom and shower, a sunroom that gets super warm during the day (prime sunbathing spot), and a very nice hostess and team. The big news: his first glimpse of Everest, peeking out from behind Lhotse’s ridge. Ama Dablam dominated the views all day, and a yak shared the trail. Day 5 by the numbers (per his Garmin): 6.40 miles, 2,270 ft of elevation gain, 3 hours 5 minutes — “absolutely beautiful day, not a cloud in the sky,” Everest, Lhotse and Ama Dablam all in view, and the body still holding up well.

photos.caption: Bundled up for the cold morning departure from Tengboche — the face covering gives sun protection and warms and moistens the thin air.
First glimpse of Everest, peeking from behind Lhotse’s ridge (Lhotse on the right).
Tyler with Ama Dablam behind.

A chorten with Ama Dablam rising behind it. The Eyes of Buddha gaze out in the four directions — a symbol of the Buddha's all-seeing wisdom, watchfulness, and compassion for the world. The curl between them is the Nepali character for 'one,' a reminder that everything is connected.
On the trail with Ama Dablam ahead.
Mani stones and cairns on the way to Dingboche.
A yak on the trail.

message: Day 6: acclimatization day in Dingboche — and what a day. Tyler climbed to Ngargjung, a 16,600-foot summit above the village: “The views are unreal and I feel so blessed to be here.” Prayer flags at the top, Ama Dablam in black and white, glacier-carved valleys, and Dingboche spread out below. The descent was a careful one — the trail turned muddy as the sun came up, so he took it slow. “A tough climb but I still felt really good in general — it’s giving me a lot of confidence for these next few days.” Back at the lodge: the green-roofed one, with Ama Dablam towering right behind it. Day 6 by the numbers (per his Garmin): 3.59 miles, 2,795 ft of elevation gain, 2 hours 41 minutes — “higher than any point in the continental US,” lungs and legs still holding up fine, and going back down tougher than going up.

photos.caption: Prayer flags at the 16,600-ft summit.
Ama Dablam in black and white.
Made it to the top — 16,600 ft.
Glacier-carved valley from the summit ridge.
Dingboche from above on the way down.
Dingboche with Lhotse towering behind.
Tyler’s lodge — the green-roofed building on the right.
The lodge with Ama Dablam towering behind it.

message:
Day 7: Dingboche → Chukhung — “super chill hike, lots of half tundra half wetlands which was neat.” 3.50 miles, 1,627 ft of elevation gain, 1 hour 48 minutes.

Chukhung → Chukhung Ri — the highest elevation he’ll hit on the whole trek. “Brutal climb. Worth the suffering. Legs are fried but will be good to go tomorrow. Pass looks good.” 4.23 miles, 3,009 ft of elevation gain, 3 hours 5 minutes.

photos.caption: A stone hut along the trail.
Taboche, looking back toward Dingboche.
A tiny alpine wildflower on the trail.

Tyler at the Chukhung Ri summit cairn.
The rocky summit ridge.
Wind-carved clouds over a snowy summit.

message: Day 8: Chukhung → Kongma La → Lobuche. The big pass day. Tyler joined up with his Canadian friend Matthew for the crossing. Snowfields, a black-and-white world of peaks, and sun over the high valley — the views heading up were something else. At the top: the Kongma La marker stone (18,159 ft), a turquoise glacial lake, and a long look down the glacial valley toward Lobuche, today’s destination — the small cluster of buildings on the far side of the valley, left of center. Then came the glacier traverse — “genuinely the hardest part of the day. We were all so exhausted from the pass and the glacier traverse took forever.” Lots of rock hopping, since no one trusted the snow by that point of the day. Day 8 by the numbers (per his Garmin): 7.57 miles, 3,806 ft of elevation gain, 5 hours 21 minutes — “Exhausting. Like a tortoise through peanut butter. Hardest day of the trek though. Feel like a true mountain guy now.”

photos.caption: Trekkers crossing the snowfield below the pass.
Matthew, who Tyler joined up with for the pass crossing.
Sun over the high valley on the way up.
Tyler at the top, trekking poles in hand.
Tyler by a turquoise glacial lake near the top.
The turquoise lake and snowy peaks.
The glacial valley — Lobuche in the background, the small cluster of buildings on the far side of the valley, left of center.
The Kongma La marker stone — 18,159 ft.
Heading through the glacier moraine.
The long glacier traverse.

message: Day 9: Lobuche → Everest Base Camp → Lobuche. The day-hike decision paid off. Tyler stood at Everest Base Camp (5,364 m), with the icefall and the summit above. And a bonus: a kong ma — the Himalayan snowcock the nearby Kongma La pass is named after. He could see Everest quite well, including the Hillary Step. Back in Lobuche, the world’s highest bakery was playing Pitbull — truly Mr. Worldwide. Day 9 by the numbers (per his Garmin): 10.04 miles round trip, 2,595 ft of elevation gain, 4 hours 51 minutes — “Sat on a big rock. Saw the Big Rock. Day well spent.”

photos.caption: Tyler at Everest Base Camp, Everest behind.
On the Everest Base Camp rock — 5,364 m.
Everest in black and white.
A kong ma — the Himalayan snowcock the Kongma La pass is named after.
The summit of Everest.

message: Day 10: Lobuche → Dzongla. A staging day. “Muddy one today. Some nice views… Today I’m just pushing through.” Day 10 by the numbers (per his Garmin): 4.24 miles, 761 ft of elevation gain, 2 hours 7 minutes.

photos.caption: Porters on the trail past a carved mani stone.
A turquoise lake below snowy peaks.
Snowy peaks reflected in the turquoise lake.
Looking toward Thukla and a small village beyond, in a different valley.
Yellow tents in the rocky valley.

message:
Day 11: Dzongla → Cho La → Gokyo. The last high pass of the trip. Snowfields, a long line of trekkers picking their way across, and then the descent into Gokyo — turquoise lakes and the village on the shore.

He stopped at Thagnak at 11:07 AM for a snack, water, and a breather. Some trekkers spend the night there due to exhaustion. He pushed through, crossing the glacier, to reach Gokyo mid-afternoon, looking forward to some well-deserved rest, and pizza and soup for dinner.

Day 11 by the numbers: 9.88 miles, 4,331 ft of elevation gain, 6:35 moving.

Thagnak is also spelled Dragnak — Sherpa is traditionally a spoken language, so place-name spellings vary.

message: Day 12: A rest day in Gokyo — a well-earned break after the Cho La crossing. Starry skies over the ridge last night, and the village by the lake in the morning light.

photos.caption: Stars over the ridge, Gokyo
Stars over the ridge, Gokyo
Gokyo village and lake in the morning light

message: Day 13: Gokyo → Namche. The day tallied 15.4 miles, 3,613 ft of gain, 7 hours. “Mile 10/11 was absolutely diabolical after the downhill I was working with all morning.” “Made it in on fumes.” Tentative plan: back to Lukla tomorrow, if the legs allow. And to celebrate being just about done — a cheeky pint at the world’s highest Irish pub tonight.

photos.caption: A cheeky pint at the world’s highest Irish pub.
Inside the pub — “If you are drinking to forget, please pay in advance.”
